cards.camps: Two camps: some say UUIDv7's rough ordering and index clustering make it useful; others say IDs should be treated only as identifiers, not trusted for ordering.

comments.text: This is a misunderstanding of the purpose of UUIDv7. The whole point is to keep rows physically close, so you can very quickly extract an entire time range from a number of database shards, with minimal reads and compute. And be able to generate them without a centralized server. That's all there was to it, and something you'd only worry about when serving billions of records every hour. They are…

> If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index. I thought the main reason UUIDv7 was created with a time component is to keep temporally related rows together in the index pages. Randomly distributed row ids seem OK until the entire index no longer fits in RAM.

One of my favorite things about UUIDv7: the package https://pypi.org/project/uuid7/ does not implement compliant UUIDv7s, it's from a wholly incompatible draft format. That was not a fun debugging session. https://pypi.org/project/uuid-utils/ is what you want :) https://github.com/stevesimmons/uuid7/issues/1

Kind of funny title since I didn’t think UUIDv7 had any of the properties being disputed here. The reason to use UUIDv7 is because it reduces the space over which the UUID can cover at a given time, which improves write clustering. They don’t need to be strictly ordered for this, just “good enough”. I hope to god no one is actually using the timestamp portion to replace an “updated at” timestamp…

If you really need monotonic, secure/unguessable IDs, there are options like CUID2 (github.com/paralleldrive/cuid2). Older designs like ULIDs ( https://github.com/ulid/spec ) and Snowflake IDs ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake_ID ) have similar properties to UUIDv7, and potentially some advantages w.r.t. length/encoding/runtime cost/etc. But UUIDv7 has one key advantage none of those do…

cards.title: How is music possible

depth.text: an essay asks why **music can make familiar things feel new**, and whether that power grows from simple building blocks

The essay notes that musical meaning can vary by culture, then weighs explanations based on **sound-processing cues** against Schopenhauer’s idea that music reveals the **underlying Will**. It wonders whether **emergence** better explains how small actions, like plucking strings or singing together, can lead to experiences too vast to explain by their parts alone.

comments.text: I've had a theory for a while now that music is related to Kolmogorov complexity, or in other words how compressible it is. Random noise that we find unpleasant is very incompressible. On the other hand, simple sound patterns that we find boring such as Do Re Mi is very compressible. What we call music sits in the middle, and is maximizing the amount of signal. In this way, we can view humans as…
Isn't the easier explanation that music/sound/rhythms has a social function for much of human history, and since humans are social creatures, we find safety and meaning in such sounds?

The article mentioned this study: The minor third communicates sadness in speech, mirroring its use in music https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20515223/ This reminded me of how I keep hearing that major doesn't really sound happy, and minor doesn't really sound sad, it's purely cultural. (But Bouba does really sound round... :) That doesn't sound right to me, but in that case maybe the speech thing…

I tried finding this section in the sources, but I couldn't find it. I wonder what's meant by this. Could it really mean that major triads are less pleasant than all tetrachords? That's surprising, since many tetrachords contain major triads. > Major chords…

glossary.front-end: The part of a service people see and use.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.backend: The part of an app that does work behind the scenes, such as handling its data.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.JavaScript fingerprint: A way a website tries to recognize your browser from details about its settings and behavior.
glossary.instance: One separately run copy of a service, with its own operator and users.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.white flight: When white residents leave neighborhoods as they become more racially diverse.
glossary.emergent phenomenon: A big effect that appears when many small things interact, even though no single small thing has it by itself.
glossary.Will: Schopenhauer’s name for the underlying reality he thought everything expresses; the essay says music represents it directly.
glossary.Kolmogorov complexity: A way to measure how briefly you can describe a pattern; simple repeated patterns take less explaining than random noise.
glossary.injection locking: When one repeating signal nudges another into matching its timing.
glossary.minor third: A particular small gap between two musical notes; the essay says some people connect it with sadness.
glossary.tropospheric ducting: A weather-related effect that can make radio signals travel much farther than usual.
